title: Cyrus and the Well
premise: Folklorist Astrid Lockridge arrives in the drowned-hollow village of Marrow Fen to record a lullaby that locals will sing only once, never twice, and discovers that each repetition feeds something beneath the old well — a thing invited in by her great-grandmother, who traded the village's church bell for a dead child's return. When the melted bell rings at midnight, Astrid learns she is the inheritance: the debt passes down the bloodline, and the village has been keeping her family's visits secret for generations. Holding out until sunrise with the doors counted and the lights burning, she must choose between completing the bargain that would return her own lost love and breaking the cycle by singing the lullaby a final time and descending into the well herself. She breaks it — but what climbs out wearing her voice suggests some inheritances cannot be refused, only redirected.
about_author: Silas Thackeray is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent a decade cataloguing funerary records in coastal East Anglia before turning to fiction. He writes horror rooted in folk custom, insisting that every haunting in his books could plausibly be found in a county record office.

chapters.title: The Song They Sing Once
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Arriving in Marrow Fen, she coaxes the lullaby from an ancient choirwoman who warns her never to ask for it twice, then notices every house keeps its doors counted aloud at dusk. Emotional beat: scholarly fascination curdling into unease as hospitality reveals itself as ritual.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, interleaved with her great-grandmother's 1911 diary. The bell rings at midnight though it was melted down; villagers bar their doors against her specifically. She uncovers the trade — a bell for a drowned child returned — and realizes her bloodline owes the balance. Emotional beat: dread of inherited guilt.

chapters.title: Counted Doors, Burning Lights
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV through the long night. The thing beneath the well wears the voice of Edvard, the lover she lost, offering her the same bargain her great-grandmother took. Villagers who once shunned her now stand vigil outside, singing the lullaby once each to hold the line. Emotional beat: love against duty at its sharpest.

chapters.title: Sunrise, and What It Doesn't Fix
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. At the edge of dawn she sings the lullaby the final time and goes down the well to close the invitation, refusing Edvard's counterfeit. The village wakes freed, the bell silent — but a knock comes at her door in a voice only she would answer. Emotional beat: costly victory, ambiguous peace.
